clinician.final_diagnosis: Benign intraductal papilloma of the right breast
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 57-year-old postmenopausal female presented with a 3-month history of right breast swelling, pain, and bloody nipple discharge. Physical examination revealed diffuse right breast thickening and erythema without palpable masses. Diagnostic imaging (mammogram and ultrasound) identified a 7.5 cm retroareolar mass with suspicious features (BIRADS 4) and axillary lymphadenopathy with concentric cortical thickening. Initial skin punch biopsy showed inflammatory changes and neutrophils. Incision and drainage yielded purulent fluid, and the patient improved on oral antibiotics. However, the patient was lost to follow-up for one year. Upon return, she presented with a new palpable mass, nipple retraction, and persistent bloody nipple discharge. Repeat imaging showed a 4.0 x 3.5 x 1.3 cm irregular hypoechoic mass with internal vascularity in the right central inner breast. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy confirmed a benign intraductal papilloma. Wire-localized excision of the right breast mass was subsequently performed, with final surgical pathology confirming the diagnosis of benign intraductal papilloma.

Initial skin punch biopsy yielded inflammatory changes and neutrophils
Incision and drainage was performed yielding purulent fluid, with clinical improvement on oral antibiotics
Patient was lost to follow-up and returned one year later with new palpable mass, nipple retraction, and persistent bloody nipple discharge

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: While initial presentation with purulent fluid on incision and drainage suggested infection, the persistence of a mass and bloody nipple discharge after antibiotic treatment, combined with imaging findings of a discrete mass, and ultimate pathological confirmation of intraductal papilloma, indicates the initial inflammatory/infectious findings were superimposed on an underlying benign papillary lesion rather than representing primary infection.

Although initial BIRADS 4 categorization and imaging features (hypervascular mass, axillary lymphadenopathy) raised concern for malignancy, both core biopsy and final surgical pathology confirmed benign intraductal papilloma without atypia or malignant features.

final.final_diagnosis: Benign intraductal papilloma of the right breast
final.trajectory_summary: A 57-year-old postmenopausal female presented with a 3-month history of right breast swelling, pain, and bloody nipple discharge. Physical examination revealed diffuse right breast thickening and erythema without palpable masses. Diagnostic imaging (mammogram and ultrasound) identified a 7.5 cm retroareolar mass with suspicious features (BIRADS 4) and axillary lymphadenopathy with concentric cortical thickening. Initial skin punch biopsy showed inflammatory changes and neutrophils. Incision and drainage yielded purulent fluid, and the patient improved on oral antibiotics. However, the patient was lost to follow-up for one year. Upon return, she presented with a new palpable mass, nipple retraction, and persistent bloody nipple discharge. Repeat imaging showed a 4.0 x 3.5 x 1.3 cm irregular hypoechoic mass with internal vascularity in the right central inner breast. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy confirmed a benign intraductal papilloma. Wire-localized excision of the right breast mass was subsequently performed, with final surgical pathology confirming the diagnosis of benign intraductal papilloma.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with right breast swelling, pain, and bloody nipple discharge for three months

Diagnostic imaging showed a 7.5 cm retroareolar mass with skin and trabecular thickening on mammogram and a 7.5 x 6.8 x 7.1 cm hypervascular complex cystic mass with thick irregular walls on ultrasound
Initial skin punch biopsy yielded inflammatory changes and neutrophils
Incision and drainage was performed yielding purulent fluid, with clinical improvement on oral antibiotics
Patient was lost to follow-up and returned one year later with new palpable mass, nipple retraction, and persistent bloody nipple discharge
Repeat imaging at one-year return showed a 4.0 x 3.5 x 1.3 cm irregular hypoechoic mass with internal vascularity in the right central inner breast with new nipple retraction
Ultrasound-guided core biopsy confirmed benign intraductal papilloma
Wire-localized excision of the right breast mass was performed with final surgical pathology revealing benign intraductal papilloma

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: While initial presentation with purulent fluid on incision and drainage suggested infection, the persistence of a mass and bloody nipple discharge after antibiotic treatment, combined with imaging findings of a discrete mass, and ultimate pathological confirmation of intraductal papilloma, indicates the initial inflammatory/infectious findings were superimposed on an underlying benign papillary lesion rather than representing primary infection.

Although initial BIRADS 4 categorization and imaging features (hypervascular mass, axillary lymphadenopathy) raised concern for malignancy, both core biopsy and final surgical pathology confirmed benign intraductal papilloma without atypia or malignant features.
